column1: Central Bank Communication  Inflation Expectations  and Monetary Policy

The thesis titled A Simple Model of Monetary Policy under Phillips-Curve Causal Disagreements by Ran Spiegler explores a static textbook model of monetary policy  challenging the conventional assumption that the private sector has rational expectations. Instead  it posits that the private sector forms inflation forecasts based on a misspecified subjective model that disagrees with the central bank's true model regarding the causal underpinnings of the Phillips Curve. The private sector's model is represented using a directed acyclic graph (DAG)  a concept borrowed from the AI/Statistics literature on Bayesian Networks. This representation allows for the modeling of causal relationships between economic variables.

The central focus of the thesis is on how the private sector's incorrect causal model can lead to rigid inflation forecasts  which in turn causes an attenuation effect in the central bank's optimal policy. This effect is particularly sensitive to the noisiness of the true inflation-output equations. The thesis highlights that when the private sector's model reverses the direction of causality between inflation and output  the central bank's response to the inflation target becomes weaker compared to the rational-expectations benchmark.

The thesis delves into the historical context of the Phillips Curve  noting that different forms of the curve have been interpreted causally in various ways. For instance  when inflation is the dependent variable  the causal narrative often involves how changes in unemployment affect inflation. Conversely  when unemployment or output is the dependent variable  the narrative shifts to how inflation impacts real variables. This distinction is crucial as it influences how the private sector forms its inflation forecasts.

Spiegler's work incorporates the private sector's expectations into a variant of the static textbook model of central-bank policy. The central bank aims to minimize a quadratic loss function of the deviations of output and inflation from their targets. The output target is fixed  while the inflation target is random. The central bank's policy instrument is chosen in response to the inflation target  balancing the deviation of inflation from its moving target against the deviation of output from its fixed target. The Phillips Curve links these deviations  with output deviations depending on the private sector's inflation forecast.

The analysis yields two key insights. First  the private sector's incorrect causal model can lead to rigid inflation forecasts  resulting in monetary-policy attenuation. Second  the variance of the noise terms in the inflation-output equations plays a significant role in the rigid-forecast effect  especially when the private sector's model reverses the direction of causality between inflation and output. The thesis emphasizes that while rational expectations render the variance of noise terms irrelevant for the private sector's forecast and the central bank's policy  a misspecified model changes this dynamic. The variance of noise terms subtly affects the private sector's inflation forecast and  consequently  central-bank policy.

Overall  the thesis provides a nuanced understanding of how disagreements over the causal interpretation of the Phillips Curve can impact monetary policy  highlighting the importance of considering the private sector's subjective models in policy formulation.
